gloss: A self-contained set of rooms on one floor of a larger building.
usage: The standard everyday word across the UK; 'apartment' sounds estate-agent speak or American.
pragmatic_note: Upmarket developers increasingly say 'apartment' to sound luxurious, but most people still say 'flat'.
pitfall: Not to be confused with 'flat' meaning a punctured tyre, which Britons call 'a flat tyre' or 'a puncture'.
examples: We've just bought a two-bedroom flat in Leeds.
Her flat's on the third floor with no lift.

gloss: A building divided into many separate flats.
usage: Everyday term for any residential building of flats, from four-storey to high-rise.
examples: They live in a block of flats near the station.
The new block of flats has a roof garden.

gloss: A very tall block of flats, often built as council housing.
usage: Used especially for post-war high-rise social housing in British cities.
pragmatic_note: The term can carry connotations of 1960s council estates rather than luxury living.
examples: She grew up on the fourteenth floor of a tower block.
Several tower blocks were demolished in the regeneration.

gloss: A compartment that carries people between the floors of a building.
usage: The only normal word in the UK; 'elevator' sounds distinctly American.
pitfall: 'Give someone a lift' means drive them somewhere, not carry them upstairs.
examples: The lift's out of order, so we'll have to take the stairs.
Take the lift to the fourth floor.

gloss: The floor of a building level with the street.
usage: Standard in buildings, shops and lifts, where it is labelled 'G' or '0'.
pitfall: Americans call this the first floor, so British floor numbers are one lower than American ones.
examples: The café is on the ground floor.
We'd prefer a ground-floor flat with a garden.

gloss: The floor immediately above the ground floor.
usage: Standard British floor numbering in homes, offices and shops.
pitfall: A British 'first floor' is an American 'second floor' — a common source of missed meetings.
examples: The bedrooms are all on the first floor.
Her office is on the first floor, just up the stairs.

gloss: One level or floor of a building.
usage: Used for counting the floors of a building, especially in compound adjectives.
pitfall: The British spelling is 'storey', plural 'storeys'; 'story' is a tale.
examples: It's a three-storey Victorian house.
The building is twelve storeys high.

gloss: A person or business that arranges the sale or letting of property.
usage: The everyday word for anyone selling houses; the office is 'the estate agent's'.
pragmatic_note: Estate agents have a slightly comic reputation in Britain for upbeat jargon like 'compact' or 'characterful'.
pitfall: 'Realtor' is not used in the UK.
examples: We've put the house on the market with a local estate agent.
The estate agent's description said 'cosy', which meant tiny.

gloss: A business that finds tenants for landlords and manages rented property.
usage: Standard term in the private rental market; often the same firm as the estate agent.
examples: The letting agent wants references from my employer.
Call the letting agent if the boiler breaks.

gloss: A person who owns a property and rents it to tenants.
usage: Used of anyone renting out a home; a woman may be called a 'landlady'.
pragmatic_note: In Britain 'landlord' also means the person who runs a pub.
examples: Our landlord still hasn't fixed the leaking tap.
Have you told the landlord you're moving out?

gloss: A sign showing a property is available to rent.
usage: Seen on boards outside houses and in adverts; the verb 'let' means rent out.
pitfall: Do not confuse with 'toilet' when read aloud: say 'to let' with a clear pause.
examples: There's a 'To Let' sign outside number twelve.
Flats to let in the city centre are scarce.

gloss: To allow someone to live in your property in return for rent.
usage: Standard in property contexts: landlords 'let' a flat; tenants 'rent' it.
pitfall: Britons say the landlord 'lets' and the tenant 'rents'; 'rent out' is also fine.
examples: They let their flat while they're working abroad.
The house was let within a week.

gloss: The written contract between a landlord and a tenant.
usage: Standard legal and everyday term for a rental contract in the UK.
examples: Read the tenancy agreement carefully before you sign.
Our tenancy agreement runs for twelve months.

gloss: A person you share a flat with, each usually having a separate bedroom.
usage: The usual word among young renters; 'housemate' is used for someone sharing a house.
pitfall: In Britain a 'roommate' would share your actual bedroom, which is unusual for adults.
examples: My flatmate always leaves the washing-up.
I'm looking for a new flatmate from September.

gloss: An arrangement where unrelated people rent rooms in the same house.
usage: Very common for young workers in expensive cities such as London.
examples: I'm living in a house share in south London.
House shares are the only affordable option for many graduates.

gloss: A person who pays to live in a room in someone else's home.
usage: Used when the owner also lives in the house; 'take in a lodger'.
examples: We've taken in a lodger to help with the mortgage.
The lodger has the back bedroom.

gloss: A house joined to one other house by a shared wall.
usage: One of the most common British house types, especially in the suburbs.
pragmatic_note: The 'semi' is a symbol of comfortable middle-class suburban life in Britain.
pitfall: An American 'duplex' can mean two flats stacked vertically, so the match is not exact.
examples: They live in a three-bed semi-detached house.
Most houses on our road are semi-detached.

gloss: Informal short form of a semi-detached house.
usage: Very common in conversation and property listings.
examples: We've bought a 1930s semi in the suburbs.
It's a pebble-dashed semi with a garage.

gloss: A house that stands alone, not joined to any other.
usage: Used in property listings and conversation; often seen as the most desirable house type.
examples: They've moved to a big detached house in the country.
Detached houses are rare in this part of town.

gloss: One of a row of houses joined together by shared side walls.
usage: Extremely common in British towns, especially Victorian housing built for workers.
pragmatic_note: Victorian terraces are now often fashionable and expensive in cities.
examples: I grew up in a two-up two-down terraced house.
Their terraced house backs onto the railway.

gloss: A terraced house at the end of the row, attached on only one side.
usage: Used in estate-agent listings and everyday conversation.
examples: Ours is an end of terrace, so we've got a side gate.
End-of-terrace houses usually have bigger gardens.

gloss: A small house with two rooms downstairs and two bedrooms upstairs.
usage: Describes traditional small terraced houses, especially in northern towns.
examples: My grandparents raised five kids in a two-up two-down.
It's a little two-up two-down near the old mill.

gloss: A house with all its rooms on one level.
usage: Common term, especially for homes popular with retired people.
pragmatic_note: Bungalows are strongly associated with retirement and seaside towns.
pitfall: In India 'bungalow' often means a large detached house; in Britain it means single-storey.
examples: My parents have moved into a bungalow by the sea.
A bungalow is easier if you struggle with stairs.

gloss: A house built and rented out by a local council at an affordable rent.
usage: Widely used, though today much social housing is run by housing associations.
pragmatic_note: Where someone grew up — a council estate or not — can still carry class connotations.
examples: She grew up in a council house in Glasgow.
Many council houses were sold to their tenants in the 1980s.

gloss: A large area of housing built by a local council.
usage: Common, neutral description, though it can carry class stereotypes.
pragmatic_note: Avoid using it as shorthand for a rough area; it can sound snobbish.
examples: He grew up on a council estate in Manchester.
The council estate has been completely renovated.

gloss: A planned area of houses built together, publicly or privately.
usage: Used for both modern private developments and council-built areas.
examples: They live on a new housing estate on the edge of town.
The housing estate has its own primary school.

gloss: A single rented room used for both living and sleeping, with shared facilities.
usage: Common from the 1960s to 1990s; now rarer and associated with student or cheap living.
pragmatic_note: 'Bedsit land' evokes rather bleak, lonely city living.
examples: I lived in a tiny bedsit when I first moved to London.
The bedsit had a sink and a single gas ring.

gloss: A flat with one main room for living and sleeping, plus a kitchen area and bathroom.
usage: Standard term in property listings and conversation.
examples: I'm renting a studio flat near work.
Studio flats are popular with young professionals.

gloss: A flat on two floors of a larger building, with its own front door.
usage: Common in British property listings; pronounced 'may-zuh-NET'.
examples: We live in a maisonette above a row of shops.
The maisonette has its own entrance at the side.

gloss: A self-contained flat within or attached to a house, often for an elderly relative.
usage: Common informal term; 'annexe' is the estate-agent word.
examples: We've converted the garage into a granny flat for Mum.
The house comes with a granny flat at the back.

gloss: An extra building or extension attached to a main house.
usage: Used in property listings for a self-contained extra living space.
pitfall: British spelling usually has the final 'e'; American is 'annex'.
examples: The property has a separate annexe for guests.
Her mother lives in the annexe.

gloss: A small, usually old house, typically in the countryside.
usage: Used widely, often with romantic connotations of rural life.
pragmatic_note: 'Cottagey' or 'chocolate-box cottage' suggests picture-postcard charm.
examples: We rented a cottage in the Lake District for a week.
It's a thatched cottage with roses round the door.

gloss: A row of houses converted from old stables, set in a small street or yard.
usage: Mainly found in London and other older cities; often expensive and sought-after.
pitfall: It is singular and plural: 'a mews house', 'in the mews'. Pronounced 'mewz'.
examples: They live in a lovely mews house in Kensington.
The mews is cobbled and very quiet.

gloss: A recently built house or flat.
usage: Common in property talk, sometimes contrasted with older 'period' properties.
pragmatic_note: Some Britons are snobbish about new builds, preferring 'character' properties.
examples: We bought a new build, so there's no work to do.
New builds often have quite small gardens.

gloss: A house in poor condition that needs renovating.
usage: Common informal term in property talk and TV shows.
examples: We bought a doer-upper and did it up ourselves.
It's a real doer-upper, but the location's perfect.

gloss: To repair and redecorate a house or room.
usage: Very common phrasal verb in everyday conversation.
examples: They're doing up the kitchen this summer.
He makes money buying old houses and doing them up.

gloss: Doing building, decorating or repairs yourself rather than paying a professional.
usage: Hugely popular British pastime; a 'DIY store' sells tools and materials.
pragmatic_note: Britons often joke about botched DIY jobs; being 'handy' is admired.
examples: My dad spends every weekend doing DIY.
The shelf fell down — that's what you get with my DIY.

gloss: Modern household equipment such as central heating or a dishwasher.
usage: Slightly old-fashioned but still heard, often jokingly, as in 'all mod cons'.
examples: The cottage is rustic but has all mod cons.
It's tiny, but it comes with all the mod cons.

gloss: Of a seller: to accept a higher offer after already agreeing a sale with someone else.
usage: A common worry in the English property market, where offers are not binding until contracts are exchanged.
examples: We were gazumped at the last minute.
Sellers rarely gazump in a slow market.

gloss: A linked series of buyers and sellers, each depending on the next sale.
usage: Often just called 'the chain'; being 'chain-free' is a selling point.
examples: The property chain collapsed when one buyer pulled out.
We're chain-free, so we can move quickly.

gloss: To leave one home and go to live in another.
usage: The standard British phrase; Americans usually just say 'move'.
examples: We're moving house next month.
Moving house is famously stressful.

gloss: The business of moving people's furniture to a new home.
usage: Used in 'removal van', 'removal men' and 'removals firm'.
pitfall: Americans say 'movers'; in Britain 'movers' is rarely used.
examples: We've booked a removals firm for Saturday.
The removal men were brilliant with the piano.

gloss: A person employed to look after a building, such as a school or block of flats.
usage: Used for schools, churches and blocks of flats.
pitfall: 'Janitor' is American or Scottish; 'caretaker' is the normal English word.
examples: Ask the caretaker to unlock the bike store.
The school caretaker fixed the radiator.

gloss: A person who lives next door or nearby.
usage: Universal; note the British spelling with 'our'.
pragmatic_note: Good relations with 'next door' are valued, but Britons tend to keep a polite distance.
examples: Our neighbours took in a parcel for us.
The new neighbours seem very nice.

gloss: The private land around a house, usually with grass and plants.
usage: Britons say 'garden' even for a small paved area behind a house.
pragmatic_note: Gardening is a national passion; people take pride in their front gardens.
pitfall: In Britain a 'yard' is a small paved area, often at the back of a terraced house.
examples: The kids are playing in the garden.
We've got a small garden at the back.

gloss: The garden behind a house.
usage: The usual phrase for the garden at the rear of a home.
examples: We had a barbecue in the back garden.
Their back garden backs onto a park.

gloss: The garden between a house and the street.
usage: Common in suburbs; often small and carefully kept.
examples: Lots of people have paved over their front gardens for parking.
Her front garden is full of roses.

gloss: In Britain, a small paved or concrete area next to a house.
usage: Used for small outdoor areas behind terraced houses, not grassy gardens.
pitfall: An American 'yard' is a British 'garden'; a British 'yard' usually has no grass.
examples: The bins are kept in the back yard.
There's just a small yard behind the terrace.

gloss: A small plot of rented land for growing vegetables, usually owned by the council.
usage: Popular with retired people and keen gardeners; waiting lists can be long.
pragmatic_note: Allotments are a cherished British tradition dating back to the nineteenth century.
examples: Dad spends every Sunday at his allotment.
We grow all our own potatoes on the allotment.

gloss: A simple wooden hut in a garden, used for storing tools.
usage: Almost every British garden has one; men retreating to 'the shed' is a cliché.
pragmatic_note: The shed is affectionately seen as a private hobby space, especially for older men.
examples: The lawnmower's in the shed.
He's built a workshop in his garden shed.

gloss: A glass-walled room built onto a house, used as living space.
usage: Very common extension on British suburban homes.
pitfall: In the US 'conservatory' often means a music school; in Britain it is usually a glass room.
examples: We have breakfast in the conservatory.
The conservatory's freezing in winter and boiling in summer.

gloss: The space under the roof of a house, often used for storage.
usage: The everyday British word; 'attic' is also used, especially for a converted room.
pitfall: An American 'loft' is often a converted industrial apartment.
examples: The Christmas decorations are up in the loft.
We're having the loft insulated.

gloss: An underground room in a house, used for storage.
usage: Used for older houses; 'basement' is used when it is a living space.
examples: The coal used to be kept in the cellar.
They've turned the cellar into a gym.

gloss: A very small bedroom, originally for storing boxes and luggage.
usage: Common in British houses, often over the stairs or front door.
examples: The baby's sleeping in the box room for now.
I work from home in the box room.

gloss: A bedroom not normally used, kept for guests or storage.
usage: The standard British term; 'guest room' sounds more like a hotel.
examples: You can stay in the spare room.
The spare room's full of junk.

gloss: A bathroom joined directly to a bedroom.
usage: Very common in property listings and hotel descriptions.
pitfall: Pronounced 'on sweet' in British English.
examples: The main bedroom has an en suite.
Is there an en-suite shower?

gloss: A room in a house for the washing machine, tumble dryer and other appliances.
usage: Common in larger family homes; a valued feature in listings.
examples: The washing machine's in the utility room.
We'd love a house with a utility room.

gloss: The area at the top of the stairs from which the upstairs rooms open.
usage: Standard word in British homes.
examples: The airing cupboard is on the landing.
Leave the landing light on, please.

gloss: The main room for relaxing in a house.
usage: Very common, though some people consider it less refined than 'sitting room'.
pragmatic_note: Choice between 'lounge', 'sitting room' and 'living room' has historically been a class marker.
examples: Come through to the lounge.
We've repainted the lounge.

gloss: The main room in a house for sitting and relaxing.
usage: Common, slightly more traditional or upper-middle-class choice than 'lounge'.
examples: Tea's in the sitting room.
The sitting room overlooks the garden.

gloss: The main living room at the front of a house.
usage: Common especially in older terraced houses and in northern England.
pragmatic_note: Historically the 'best' room kept tidy for visitors.
examples: We only used the front room at Christmas.
Put the telly in the front room.

gloss: Informal word for a television or for television in general.
usage: Extremely common in casual speech across all classes.
examples: What's on the telly tonight?
He fell asleep in front of the telly.

gloss: A narrow wooden board running along the bottom of an interior wall.
usage: Standard British term in decorating and DIY.
examples: I need to paint the skirting boards.
There's a mouse hole behind the skirting board.

gloss: Carpet cut to cover the whole floor of a room.
usage: Common in British homes, especially bedrooms and stairs.
examples: The bedrooms all have fitted carpets.
We pulled up the fitted carpet to find floorboards.

gloss: A piece of furniture or built-in space with a door, used for storage.
usage: Used for kitchen storage, built-in storage and small rooms such as 'the airing cupboard'.
pitfall: Pronounced 'KUB-uhd' — the 'p' is silent.
examples: The mugs are in the cupboard above the kettle.
There's a cupboard under the stairs.

gloss: A warm cupboard containing a hot-water tank, used for drying and storing linen.
usage: A familiar feature of older British homes with hot-water cylinders.
examples: The towels are in the airing cupboard.
Leave the bread dough in the airing cupboard to rise.

gloss: A building for keeping a car; also a place that repairs cars.
usage: Commonly pronounced 'GARR-ij' or 'GARR-ahzh' in Britain; stress is on the first syllable.
pitfall: Americans stress the second syllable: 'guh-RAHZH'.
examples: The car won't fit in the garage — it's full of junk.
We're converting the garage into an office.

gloss: A small covered or enclosed area at the front door of a house.
usage: In Britain usually a small enclosed entrance rather than a large veranda.
pitfall: An American porch is often a large open veranda where people sit.
examples: Leave the parcel in the porch.
We've had a little porch built on the front.

gloss: A raised wooden platform in a garden.
usage: Very common in British gardens since the 1990s.
examples: We've put decking in the back garden.
The decking gets slippery in the rain.

gloss: Windows with two layers of glass to keep heat in and noise out.
usage: Standard feature mentioned in property listings and sales calls.
examples: The house has double glazing throughout.
Double glazing has really cut our heating bills.

gloss: Informal word for a toilet.
usage: Very common, friendly and inoffensive across all classes.
pragmatic_note: 'Loo' is the polite, middle-of-the-road choice between 'toilet' and 'lavatory'.
examples: Where's the loo?
I'll just nip to the loo before we go.

gloss: A bowl for urinating and defecating, or the room containing it.
usage: The most common neutral word; ask 'Where's the toilet?' in shops or restaurants.
pragmatic_note: Britons ask directly for 'the toilet'; American euphemisms like 'restroom' sound odd.
pitfall: Some traditionally consider 'toilet' slightly non-U compared with 'loo' or 'lavatory'.
examples: Excuse me, where are the toilets?
The toilets are downstairs on the left.

gloss: A room containing a bath or shower and usually a basin.
usage: In Britain it names the room with the bath, which may or may not include the toilet.
pitfall: Asking for 'the bathroom' in a British restaurant may confuse people; ask for 'the toilet' or 'the loo'.
examples: The bathroom's at the top of the stairs.
We're having the bathroom refitted.

gloss: A toilet; a formal or traditional word.
usage: Used on signs, in formal writing and by some older or upper-class speakers.
examples: The lavatory is at the end of the corridor.
Lavatories are located on each floor.

gloss: A small room with a toilet and basin on the ground floor.
usage: A desirable feature in British family homes.
examples: We've squeezed a downstairs loo under the stairs.
Is there a downstairs loo?

gloss: A room for leaving coats; in homes, often a small downstairs toilet.
usage: Used in theatres and restaurants for coats, and in estate-agent speak for a downstairs toilet.
examples: You can leave your coat in the cloakroom.
The house has a cloakroom off the hall.

gloss: A large container you fill with water and sit in to wash.
usage: Britons 'have a bath'; the verb 'to bath' means to wash a baby or someone in a bath.
pitfall: Americans 'take a bath'; Britons usually 'have a bath'. Pronounced 'bahth' in RP.
examples: I'm going to have a long hot bath.
Can you bath the baby tonight?

gloss: A device for controlling the flow of water from a pipe.
usage: The only everyday word in the UK; 'faucet' is not used.
examples: Don't leave the tap running.
The hot tap in the bathroom drips.

gloss: A bowl in a bathroom, fixed to the wall, for washing hands and face.
usage: Often 'washbasin' or 'hand basin'; 'sink' is used for the kitchen.
examples: Rinse your razor in the basin.
There's a basin in the corner of the bedroom.

gloss: The hole in a bath or sink through which water drains away.
usage: Everyday word, often heard in 'down the plughole'.
examples: The plughole's blocked with hair again.
My ring went down the plughole.

gloss: A shower with an electric pump that boosts water pressure.
usage: Common in British homes, where mains water pressure can be low.
examples: We've installed a power shower.
Nothing beats a power shower in the morning.

gloss: A small square of towelling used for washing your face and body.
usage: Common in Britain; 'face cloth' is also used.
pitfall: 'Flannel' also means a soft fabric and, informally, evasive talk.
examples: Pass me a flannel, would you?
She wiped the baby's face with a flannel.

gloss: Paper for wiping yourself after using the toilet, or one roll of it.
usage: The everyday British term; 'loo roll' is the informal version.
examples: We're out of toilet roll.
Can you grab some loo roll from the shop?

gloss: Liquid soap for use in the shower.
usage: The usual British name on packaging and in conversation.
examples: I've run out of shower gel.
The hotel gave us mini bottles of shower gel.

gloss: A small bag for carrying toothbrush, soap and toiletries when travelling.
usage: Common British term; 'sponge bag' is older and 'toiletry bag' is also used.
examples: Have you packed your wash bag?
My toothpaste leaked all over my wash bag.

gloss: Soft fluffy cotton used for cleaning skin or removing make-up.
usage: Standard word in the UK; individual pieces are 'cotton wool balls' or 'pads'.
pragmatic_note: 'Wrap someone in cotton wool' means to overprotect them.
pitfall: Americans say 'cotton balls' or 'absorbent cotton'.
examples: Dab it on with a bit of cotton wool.
We need more cotton wool pads.

gloss: A short stick with cotton wool on each end, for cleaning ears or applying make-up.
usage: Standard British term; 'Q-tip' is an American brand name.
examples: Don't put cotton buds in your ears.
Use a cotton bud to clean the corners.

gloss: A small adhesive strip with a pad, used to cover cuts.
usage: The everyday British word; 'sticking plaster' is fuller and older.
pitfall: 'Band-Aid' is a brand name and sounds American in the UK.
examples: Have you got a plaster? I've cut my finger.
Put a plaster on that blister.

gloss: A common mild painkiller, sold without prescription.
usage: The standard word; Britons say 'take a couple of paracetamol'.
pitfall: Americans know it as acetaminophen or by the brand Tylenol.
examples: Take a couple of paracetamol and lie down.
Have we got any paracetamol in the house?

gloss: Coloured or clear liquid painted on fingernails or toenails.
usage: Common British term; 'nail polish' is also widely used.
examples: She's painting her nails with red nail varnish.
Have you got any nail varnish remover?

gloss: A heated tool with two plates used to straighten hair.
usage: Everyday British term; often just 'straighteners'.
examples: Did I leave my hair straighteners on?
Her straighteners are always plugged in.

gloss: A small folded metal pin for holding hair in place.
usage: Standard British term; 'kirby grip' is also common.
examples: I need a hairgrip to keep my fringe back.
There are hairgrips all over the bathroom floor.

gloss: An elastic band, often decorated, for tying back hair.
usage: Common in the north of England and Scotland; elsewhere 'hairband' or 'hair tie'.
examples: Have you got a spare hair bobble?
She keeps a hair bobble on her wrist.

gloss: A flexible curved band worn over the head to hold hair back.
usage: Traditional British term, named after Alice in Wonderland illustrations.
pragmatic_note: Can suggest a traditional, slightly posh style.
examples: She wore a velvet Alice band.
Put an Alice band in to keep your hair out of your eyes.

gloss: Hair cut to hang over the forehead.
usage: The standard word at the hairdresser's.
pitfall: Americans say 'bangs'; in Britain 'fringe' also means the edge of something.
examples: I'm thinking of having a fringe cut in.
Your fringe needs a trim.

gloss: A length of hair divided into three strands and woven together.
usage: Standard British word; pronounced 'plat', rhyming with 'cat'.
pitfall: Pronounced 'plat', not 'plate'.
examples: She wears her hair in two plaits.
Can you plait my hair for school?

gloss: A large kitchen appliance with an oven and a hob.
usage: The usual British word for the whole appliance.
pitfall: A 'cooker' in Britain is an appliance, never a person who cooks.
examples: We need a new cooker — the oven's packed up.
The cooker's gas, not electric.

gloss: The flat top of a cooker, or a separate unit, with rings or zones for pans.
usage: Standard in British kitchens: gas hob, induction hob, ceramic hob.
examples: Leave the soup simmering on the hob.
We've got an induction hob now.

gloss: The part of a cooker that cooks food with direct heat from above.
usage: Britons 'grill' toast or bacon under the grill inside the cooker.
pitfall: An American 'grill' is usually a barbecue; the British 'grill' heats from above.
examples: Pop the cheese on toast under the grill.
Grill the bacon for five minutes each side.

gloss: The flat work surface in a kitchen.
usage: Standard British term in kitchen design and everyday speech.
examples: Wipe down the worktop when you've finished.
We've chosen oak worktops for the kitchen.

gloss: The fitted cupboards that make up a kitchen.
usage: Common in DIY and kitchen design; 'kitchen cupboards' also used.
examples: We've repainted the kitchen units.
The wall units are a bit high for me.

gloss: An electric fan that removes steam or cooking smells from a room.
usage: Found in kitchens and bathrooms; 'cooker hood' for the one over the hob.
examples: Put the extractor fan on — it's getting steamy.
The bathroom extractor fan's very noisy.

gloss: An electric jug for boiling water, used many times a day.
usage: Essential in every British home and office; 'put the kettle on' signals tea.
pragmatic_note: 'I'll put the kettle on' is a classic British gesture of welcome or comfort.
pitfall: Many Americans heat water on the stove; an electric kettle is a British basic.
examples: I'll put the kettle on.
The kettle's just boiled.

gloss: A combined refrigerator and freezer in one tall unit.
usage: Common British term for the standard kitchen appliance.
examples: We need a bigger fridge-freezer.
The fridge-freezer's making a funny noise.

gloss: A cool room or large cupboard for storing food.
usage: Somewhat traditional; 'pantry' is also common in Britain.
examples: The jam's in the larder.
Old cottages often have a stone larder.

gloss: The dirty plates, pans and cutlery to be washed, or the act of washing them.
usage: Britons 'do the washing-up' after meals.
pragmatic_note: Offering to do the washing-up is a classic polite gesture for a dinner guest.
pitfall: Americans 'wash up' meaning wash their hands; in Britain 'wash up' means do the dishes.
examples: I'll do the washing-up if you dry.
There's a mountain of washing-up in the sink.

gloss: Liquid detergent for washing dishes by hand.
usage: Standard British term found on every kitchen windowsill.
examples: We're out of washing-up liquid.
Just a squirt of washing-up liquid is enough.

gloss: A plastic bowl placed in the sink for washing dishes.
usage: Very common in British kitchens.
examples: Fill the washing-up bowl with hot water.
Leave the pan to soak in the washing-up bowl.

gloss: A sloping surface next to the sink where washed dishes are left to dry.
usage: Standard in British kitchens.
examples: Leave the plates on the draining board.
The draining board's full of pans.

gloss: A cloth for drying dishes after washing them.
usage: Universal in Britain; souvenir tea towels are a classic gift.
pragmatic_note: Printed tea towels are a stock British souvenir from gift shops.
examples: Grab a tea towel and give me a hand.
She hung the tea towel over the oven door.

gloss: Absorbent paper on a roll, used for wiping up spills.
usage: The standard British term; 'kitchen towel' is also used.
examples: Pass the kitchen roll — I've spilt my tea.
Drain the bacon on some kitchen roll.

gloss: Thin clear plastic film used to cover food.
usage: Standard British term; also written 'clingfilm'.
pitfall: Americans may say 'Saran wrap', a brand name.
examples: Cover the bowl with cling film.
Wrap the sandwiches in cling film.

gloss: Thin metal sheet used to wrap or cover food.
usage: Common everyday term; 'kitchen foil' or 'aluminium foil' are also used.
pitfall: British spelling and pronunciation is 'aluminium', with five syllables.
examples: Cover the turkey with tin foil.
Wrap the leftovers in tin foil.

gloss: A thick padded glove for handling hot dishes.
usage: Standard British term.
examples: Use an oven glove — the tray's boiling.
Where are the oven gloves?

gloss: A device for opening tins of food.
usage: Common British term; 'can opener' is also understood.
pitfall: Britons call food cans 'tins', though drinks come in 'cans'.
examples: Have you seen the tin opener?
The tin opener's in the drawer by the sink.

gloss: A flat kitchen utensil with slots, used for lifting and turning food.
usage: Traditional British name for the turner used for eggs and fish.
pitfall: Not only for fish; it lifts anything from a pan.
examples: Use the fish slice to flip the pancakes.
Pass me the fish slice, would you?

gloss: A container with a handle and a lip, for pouring liquids.
usage: Standard British word: water jug, milk jug, measuring jug.
examples: Can we have a jug of water, please?
Pour the milk into the jug.

gloss: Knives, forks and spoons used for eating.
usage: The normal British word; 'silverware' would mean actual silver.
examples: The cutlery's in the top drawer.
Can you lay the cutlery for six?

gloss: Plates, cups, bowls and similar dishes.
usage: Standard British word for everyday tableware.
examples: We've bought new crockery for the flat.
Mind the crockery when you move that box.

gloss: Waste material that you throw away.
usage: The standard British word; also used to mean 'nonsense' or 'poor quality'.
pragmatic_note: 'That's rubbish!' is a very common mild way to say something is bad.
pitfall: 'Trash' and 'garbage' sound American.
examples: Can you take the rubbish out?
The rubbish is collected on Tuesdays.

gloss: A container for rubbish, indoors or outdoors.
usage: The everyday British word for any waste container.
examples: Put it in the bin.
The kitchen bin's full again.

gloss: A large outdoor container for household rubbish.
usage: Somewhat old-fashioned; most people now just say 'bin' or 'wheelie bin'.
examples: The foxes knocked over the dustbin again.
Put the dustbin out by the gate.

gloss: A large plastic rubbish bin with wheels and a hinged lid.
usage: Universal in Britain; councils give each household colour-coded wheelie bins.
examples: Don't forget to put the wheelie bin out tonight.
Our wheelie bin is blue for recycling.

gloss: A large plastic bag for lining a bin or holding rubbish.
usage: Standard British term; 'bin liner' is also common.
examples: Tie up the bin bag and take it outside.
We need some more bin bags.

gloss: The day of the week when the council collects household rubbish.
usage: Part of British domestic routine; recycling and general waste may alternate weeks.
examples: Is it bin day tomorrow?
I always forget it's bin day.

gloss: The council workers who collect household rubbish.
usage: Common informal term; official term is 'refuse collectors'.
examples: The bin men didn't take our recycling.
The bin men come early on Thursdays.

gloss: A large open metal container for building rubbish, collected by lorry.
usage: Common sight outside houses being renovated.
pragmatic_note: 'Skip diving' means rescuing useful things from skips.
pitfall: A US 'dumpster' is usually closed; a British skip is open-topped.
examples: We've hired a skip for the kitchen refit.
Someone's dumped a sofa in our skip.

gloss: To clean a floor with a vacuum cleaner; also the cleaner itself.
usage: Very common British verb and noun, whatever the brand of machine.
pitfall: Americans say 'vacuum'; in Britain 'hoover' is the everyday verb.
examples: I'll hoover the lounge before they arrive.
Where's the hoover?

gloss: A short brush and flat pan for sweeping up dirt.
usage: The usual British phrase for this pair.
examples: Get the dustpan and brush — I've dropped a glass.
The dustpan and brush are under the sink.

gloss: Powdered detergent for washing clothes.
usage: Common British term; liquid versions are 'washing liquid' or 'liquid detergent'.
examples: We're out of washing powder.
This washing powder is good for sensitive skin.

gloss: A liquid added during washing to make clothes soft.
usage: Common British term; 'fabric softener' also used.
examples: Add some fabric conditioner to the drawer.
I love the smell of this fabric conditioner.

gloss: Clothes that need washing or have just been washed.
usage: Britons 'do the washing' and 'hang the washing out'.
examples: I need to do a load of washing.
Can you bring the washing in? It's raining.

gloss: A rope or wire outside on which wet washing is hung to dry.
usage: Very common in British gardens.
examples: Hang the sheets on the washing line.
The washing line's sagging.

gloss: A small clip used to fix washing to a line.
usage: The standard British term; often just 'peg'.
examples: Pass me some clothes pegs.
The wind blew the shirt off despite the pegs.

gloss: A folding frame on which washing is hung to dry indoors.
usage: Common term; 'airer' is also widely used.
examples: Put the clothes horse in front of the radiator.
The clothes horse takes up half the lounge.

gloss: An electric machine that dries washing by turning it in hot air.
usage: Standard British term, often just 'the dryer'.
examples: Don't put that jumper in the tumble dryer.
Our tumble dryer takes ages.

gloss: A shop with coin-operated washing machines and dryers for public use.
usage: Standard British term; less common now most homes have washing machines.
examples: I used to take my washing to the launderette.
There's a launderette at the end of the road.

gloss: A metal panel filled with hot water from the boiler, used to heat a room.
usage: The standard way British homes are heated; often just 'the radiators'.
pitfall: Pronounced 'RAY-dee-ay-tuh' in British English.
examples: Put the wet gloves on the radiator.
Can you bleed the radiators? They're cold at the top.

gloss: A system that heats a whole building from one boiler through pipes and radiators.
usage: Standard in British homes; 'the heating' for short.
pragmatic_note: Debating when to 'put the heating on' in autumn is a British household ritual.
examples: Shall we put the heating on?
The house has gas central heating.

gloss: The appliance that heats water for a home's radiators and taps.
usage: Every British home with central heating has one; breakdowns are a winter dread.
pitfall: Americans often heat with a 'furnace' that blows air; British boilers heat water.
examples: The boiler's broken again.
We need a gas engineer to service the boiler.

gloss: A boiler that heats water directly on demand, with no storage tank.
usage: The most common type in modern British homes.
examples: We've had a combi boiler fitted.
With a combi boiler you don't need a hot water tank.

gloss: An electric element inside a hot water tank used to heat water.
usage: Found in older homes; often just 'the immersion'.
pragmatic_note: 'Have you left the immersion on?' is a classic household worry about bills.
examples: Switch the immersion on if you want a bath.
Did you leave the immersion on all day?

gloss: The fitting in a wall into which you put an electric plug.
usage: Everyday British term; 'socket' and 'power point' are also used.
pragmatic_note: British sockets have their own switches, which visitors often forget to turn on.
pitfall: Americans say 'outlet'; in Britain an 'outlet' is usually a shop.
examples: Is there a plug socket near the bed?
Switch it on at the plug socket.

gloss: The device with pins on an electric lead that fits into a socket.
usage: British plugs have three rectangular pins and a fuse inside.
pitfall: 'Plug' also means the stopper for a bath or sink.
examples: You'll need an adaptor for a UK plug.
Pull the plug out before you clean it.

gloss: A length of cable with sockets at one end, to reach a distant plug socket.
usage: Standard British term; 'extension cable' is also used.
examples: Is there an extension lead for the laptop?
Don't overload the extension lead.

gloss: The flexible electric cable connecting an appliance to a plug.
usage: Everyday British word for a cable; also a dog's leash.
pitfall: Pronounced 'leed' in this sense; Americans say 'cord'.
examples: The lead on the kettle's too short.
I've forgotten my phone charger lead.

gloss: The box containing the fuses or circuit breakers for a home's electricity.
usage: Everyday term; electricians say 'consumer unit'.
examples: The power's gone — check the fuse box.
The fuse box is under the stairs.

gloss: The main supply of electricity, water or gas to a building.
usage: Used in 'mains electricity', 'mains water' and 'turn it off at the mains'.
examples: Turn the water off at the mains.
It runs on batteries or mains power.

gloss: A small portable battery-powered light.
usage: The only everyday British word; 'flashlight' sounds American.
pitfall: In Britain a torch is not on fire — that would be a 'flaming torch'.
examples: Have you got a torch? The power's gone off.
I use the torch on my phone.

gloss: A rubber container filled with hot water to warm a bed or body.
usage: A beloved winter comfort in British homes.
pragmatic_note: Hot water bottles with knitted covers are a symbol of British cosiness.
examples: I always take a hot water bottle to bed in winter.
Fill me a hot water bottle, would you?

gloss: A thick quilt filled with feathers or synthetic fibre, used as bedding.
usage: Universal in Britain since the 1970s; pronounced 'DOO-vay'.
pitfall: Pronounced 'DOO-vay': the final 't' is silent.
examples: It's cold — I've got the winter duvet out.
Shall we get a king-size duvet?

gloss: A removable fabric case that covers a duvet.
usage: Standard British term; putting one on is a notorious chore.
examples: Help me put the duvet cover on.
We've bought a new duvet cover.

gloss: A unit for measuring how warm a duvet or sleeping bag is.
usage: Used on British duvet packaging: a 13.5-tog duvet is for winter.
pitfall: Unfamiliar outside the UK and a few other countries.
examples: A 4.5-tog duvet is fine for summer.
What tog is your duvet?

gloss: A thick quilt filled with down, laid on top of the bedclothes.
usage: Old-fashioned; mostly used by older people or in period settings.
pitfall: Dated: most Britons now use a duvet.
examples: My grandmother had a pink satin eiderdown.
The bed was piled with blankets and an eiderdown.

gloss: The sheets, blankets and covers on a bed.
usage: Standard word; 'bedding' and 'bed linen' are also common.
examples: He pulled the bedclothes over his head.
Strip the bedclothes and put them in the wash.

gloss: A small table or cabinet next to a bed.
usage: The usual British term; 'bedside cabinet' is also used.
examples: My phone's on the bedside table.
She keeps a glass of water on the bedside table.

gloss: A piece of furniture with drawers for clothes.
usage: The standard British term.
pitfall: In Britain a 'dresser' is a kitchen cabinet with open shelves for plates.
examples: Your socks are in the chest of drawers.
We painted the old chest of drawers white.

gloss: A kitchen cabinet with open shelves above for displaying plates.
usage: Traditional, especially the 'Welsh dresser' in country kitchens.
pitfall: In the US a 'dresser' is a chest of drawers for clothes.
examples: The plates are displayed on the Welsh dresser.
We've got an old pine dresser in the kitchen.

gloss: A tall cupboard for hanging clothes.
usage: Standard British word; also means a person's collection of clothes.
pitfall: Britons rarely say 'closet' for a cupboard.
examples: Hang your coat in the wardrobe.
We need a bigger wardrobe.

gloss: A long upholstered seat for two or more people.
usage: The most common neutral British word.
pragmatic_note: 'Sofa', 'settee' and 'couch' have traditionally carried subtle class connotations.
examples: We fell asleep on the sofa.
They've bought a new corner sofa.

gloss: A sofa.
usage: Common, especially in the north of England and among older speakers.
examples: Come and sit on the settee.
The cat's asleep on the settee.

gloss: Pieces of fabric hung at a window to cover it.
usage: The everyday word in Britain; 'drapes' sounds American or overly grand.
examples: Draw the curtains — it's getting dark.
We've ordered made-to-measure curtains.

gloss: Thin see-through curtains that give privacy during the day.
usage: Traditional in British homes, especially among older generations.
pragmatic_note: Twitching net curtains are a cliché of nosy neighbours.
examples: My nan still has net curtains.
The net curtains twitched as we walked past.

gloss: Furniture sold in pieces in a flat box, for assembling at home.
usage: Very common; assembling it is a stereotypical domestic struggle.
examples: We spent all Sunday building a flat-pack wardrobe.
Flat-pack furniture is cheap but fiddly.

gloss: A short pin with a flat round head, pushed in with the thumb.
usage: Standard British term.
examples: Pin the notice up with a drawing pin.
Mind you don't tread on a drawing pin.

gloss: Clear sticky tape.
usage: A trademark used generically in Britain, also as a verb.
examples: Have we got any Sellotape?
Sellotape the card to the present.

gloss: A blue reusable putty-like adhesive for sticking paper to walls.
usage: A trademark used generically; common in homes and student rooms.
pragmatic_note: Landlords often ban Blu Tack because it marks the walls.
examples: Stick the poster up with Blu Tack.
There are Blu Tack marks all over the wall.

gloss: A small block of rubber for removing pencil marks.
usage: The everyday British word, especially in schools.
pitfall: In American slang 'rubber' can mean a condom, so say 'eraser' with Americans.
examples: Can I borrow your rubber?
There's a rubber on the end of the pencil.

gloss: A ballpoint pen.
usage: A trademark used generically in Britain; pronounced 'BYE-roh'.
examples: Have you got a biro I can borrow?
Sign it in blue biro.

gloss: Letters and parcels delivered to homes; the system that delivers them.
usage: The normal British word; 'Royal Mail' is the name of the service.
pitfall: Americans say 'mail'; Britons say 'post' for the letters and 'the post' for the service.
examples: Has the post come yet?
I'll put it in the post today.

gloss: A person who delivers letters and parcels.
usage: Common everyday word; 'postie' is informal.
examples: The postman left a card through the door.
Our postman comes at about ten.

gloss: A combination of letters and numbers identifying a postal address.
usage: Used constantly in online forms and sat-navs.
pragmatic_note: Postcodes can carry connotations: a 'good postcode' suggests an affluent area.
examples: What's your postcode?
Just put the postcode into the sat nav.

gloss: A public box for posting letters.
usage: Common term; traditional red cylindrical ones are 'pillar boxes'.
pragmatic_note: The red pillar box is an iconic British street object.
pitfall: A US 'mailbox' can also be your private box at home; Britons have a 'letterbox'.
examples: There's a postbox at the end of the road.
Last collection from this postbox is at half five.

gloss: A slot in a front door through which post is delivered.
usage: Standard British term; flats may have individual post boxes in the hall.
examples: The leaflets keep coming through the letterbox.
The parcel won't fit through the letterbox.

gloss: A wrapped object sent by post.
usage: The standard British word; 'package' is also used.
examples: There's a parcel waiting for you at the sorting office.
I'll post the parcel tomorrow.

gloss: A postal service where the recipient signs to confirm delivery.
usage: Common term; officially 'Signed For' nowadays.
examples: Send it recorded delivery so we know it's arrived.
The letter came by recorded delivery.

gloss: A long flexible tube for watering the garden.
usage: Common British term, often just 'hose'.
examples: There's a hosepipe ban this summer.
Water the tomatoes with the hosepipe.

gloss: Strong scissors for cutting plant stems.
usage: Standard British gardening word; pronounced 'SEK-uh-turz'.
pitfall: Always plural, like scissors: 'a pair of secateurs'.
examples: I need my secateurs to cut back the roses.
Have you seen the secateurs?

gloss: A large shop selling plants, garden tools and outdoor furniture.
usage: A popular British weekend outing, often with a café.
pragmatic_note: A Sunday trip to the garden centre is a stereotypically British pastime.
examples: We spent Saturday at the garden centre.
The garden centre has a lovely café.

gloss: A large barrel for collecting rainwater from a roof.
usage: Common in British gardens, especially during hosepipe bans.
examples: We use the water butt for the vegetables.
The water butt's overflowing after the storm.

gloss: A knitted woollen garment for the upper body, with long sleeves.
usage: The everyday British word; 'sweater' and 'pullover' are also used.
pitfall: In the US a 'jumper' is a pinafore dress.
examples: Take a jumper — it's chilly out.
Granny knitted me a jumper for Christmas.

gloss: A sleeveless knitted jumper worn over a shirt.
usage: Traditional British meaning, though the American sense is now common too.
pitfall: To Americans a 'tank top' is a sleeveless vest top; Britons may use either sense.
examples: He wore a knitted tank top over his shirt.
Tank tops were very fashionable in the seventies.

gloss: Soft sports shoes worn for exercise or casually.
usage: The universal British word; 'sneakers' sounds American.
examples: I'll wear my trainers for the walk.
He's got a new pair of trainers.

gloss: Light canvas shoes with flat rubber soles, traditionally for school PE.
usage: Traditional British word; 'pumps' in some regions.
examples: We had to wear plimsolls for PE.
White plimsolls are back in fashion.

gloss: A garment covering the body from the waist to the ankles, with separate legs.
usage: The standard British word.
pitfall: In Britain 'pants' means underwear; say 'trousers' to avoid embarrassment.
examples: He spilt coffee on his trousers.
I need a new pair of work trousers.

gloss: Underwear covering the bottom.
usage: Everyday British word for underwear; also informal slang for 'rubbish'.
pragmatic_note: 'That's pants!' is a mild, jokey way of saying something is bad.
pitfall: False friend: in the US 'pants' means trousers. 'I like your pants' is embarrassing in Britain.
examples: I've packed enough pants and socks for a week.
He came down in just his pants.

gloss: Women's or girls' underpants.
usage: Common, slightly informal; used humorously in some expressions.
pitfall: Use only for women's underwear; in American English 'knickers' can mean knee-length breeches.
examples: She packed a few pairs of knickers.
Her knickers were drying on the radiator.

gloss: Men's underpants with a seam in the shape of an upside-down Y.
usage: Common British term, often used humorously.
examples: My dad still wears Y-fronts.
He came downstairs in his Y-fronts.

gloss: A sleeveless undergarment worn under a shirt.
usage: Standard British meaning; also a sleeveless running top.
pitfall: In the US a 'vest' is a waistcoat; British 'vests' are underwear or sportswear.
examples: Put a vest on under your shirt — it's freezing.
Runners wear vests with their numbers pinned on.

gloss: A sleeveless garment with buttons worn over a shirt, often as part of a suit.
usage: Standard British term; pronounced 'WAIST-coat' or traditionally 'WESS-kit'.
pitfall: Americans call this a 'vest', which in Britain is underwear.
examples: He wore a three-piece suit with a waistcoat.
The groom's waistcoat matched the bridesmaids' dresses.

gloss: A sleeveless padded jacket.
usage: Fashionable outdoor wear, also called a 'body warmer'; pronounced 'ZHEE-lay'.
examples: I wear a gilet for dog walks.
He was in a quilted gilet and wellies.

gloss: A long loose garment worn over nightclothes.
usage: The standard British term; 'robe' or 'bathrobe' are also used.
examples: He answered the door in his dressing gown.
I love my fluffy dressing gown.

gloss: A loose dress worn in bed by women or girls.
usage: Common informal word; 'nightdress' is the fuller form.
examples: She was in her nightie and slippers.
Put your nightie on, it's bedtime.

gloss: A loose jacket and trousers worn in bed.
usage: British spelling is 'pyjamas'; often 'PJs' informally.
pitfall: British spelling uses 'y'; pronounced 'puh-JAH-muhz' in RP.
examples: Get your pyjamas on — it's bedtime.
I spent all Sunday in my pyjamas.

gloss: Informal, childish word for pyjamas.
usage: Used affectionately, especially with children.
examples: Time to get your jim-jams on!
She came down in her jim-jams.

gloss: Waterproof rubber boots reaching almost to the knee.
usage: Very common; short for 'wellington boots'.
pragmatic_note: Wellies are associated with muddy walks, festivals and the countryside.
examples: Put your wellies on — it's muddy.
Everyone was in wellies at the festival.

gloss: Straps over the shoulders that hold trousers up.
usage: Standard British word; also means dental braces.
pitfall: In Britain 'suspenders' hold up stockings, so take care with the American word.
examples: He wore red braces with his suit.
Braces are back in fashion.

gloss: Elastic straps hanging from a belt to hold up stockings.
usage: British meaning; much less common in everyday talk than 'braces'.
pitfall: False friend: American 'suspenders' are British 'braces'.
examples: She wore stockings and suspenders in the period drama.
Suspender belts are rarely worn nowadays.

gloss: A close-fitting garment of thin nylon or wool, covering the feet, legs and hips.
usage: The standard British word.
pitfall: Americans use 'tights' for thicker opaque ones only.
examples: I've laddered my tights.
She wore black tights with her skirt.

gloss: A line of broken threads in tights or stockings.
usage: Everyday British term in clothing talk.
pitfall: Americans say a 'run' in your stockings.
examples: You've got a ladder in your tights.
My tights laddered on the train.

gloss: A waterproof coat; short for 'mackintosh'.
usage: Common, slightly traditional word for a raincoat.
pitfall: Not to be confused with the computer brand.
examples: Take your mac — it looks like rain.
He wore a beige mac and a flat cap.

gloss: A waterproof jacket, usually with a hood.
usage: Common word; informally also means an obsessive enthusiast.
pragmatic_note: Calling someone 'an anorak' means they are a geeky enthusiast.
examples: Bring an anorak — it's always raining in Wales.
He zipped up his anorak against the wind.

gloss: A lightweight waterproof jacket with a hood, often pulled over the head.
usage: Common for hiking; often 'cag' informally.
examples: Pack a cagoule for the hike.
Her cagoule folds into its own pocket.

gloss: A man's formal black jacket for evening wear, worn with a bow tie.
usage: Used on invitations as 'black tie'; often 'DJ' informally.
pragmatic_note: A 'black tie' dress code means a dinner jacket, not just a black necktie.
pitfall: 'Tuxedo' is understood but sounds American.
examples: The invitation says black tie, so I'll wear my dinner jacket.
He hired a dinner jacket for the ball.

gloss: A jumper with a high, close, folded collar.
usage: Standard British term.
pitfall: In Britain a 'turtle neck' is a lower collar; Americans use 'turtleneck' for polo necks.
examples: She wore a black polo neck and jeans.
A polo neck is warmer than a scarf.

gloss: Loose, soft trousers worn for exercise or lounging.
usage: Common British term; informally 'trackies' or 'joggers'.
examples: I just want to get home and put my tracksuit bottoms on.
He went to the shop in tracksuit bottoms.

gloss: A matching loose top and trousers worn for sport or leisure.
usage: Common British word.
examples: The team arrived in matching tracksuits.
He wears a tracksuit at the weekend.

gloss: A garment worn for swimming, especially a one-piece for women.
usage: Common British term; 'cossie' is informal and 'swimsuit' is also used.
examples: Don't forget your swimming costume.
She bought a new swimming costume for the holiday.

gloss: Informal short form of 'swimming costume'.
usage: Colloquial, mainly used with children and family.
examples: Grab your cossie, we're going to the pool.
Your cossie's still wet from yesterday.

gloss: Shorts worn by men or boys for swimming.
usage: Standard British term, often just 'trunks'.
examples: I forgot my swimming trunks.
He bought new trunks for the holiday.

gloss: The folded-up bottom edges of trouser legs.
usage: Standard British tailoring term.
pitfall: In Britain 'cuffs' are the ends of shirt sleeves.
examples: Do you want turn-ups on the trousers?
His jeans had big turn-ups.

gloss: The opening at the front of trousers, closed with a zip or buttons.
usage: Britons usually use the plural; 'flies are undone' is a gentle warning.
examples: Your flies are undone.
He quickly did up his flies.

gloss: A fastener with two rows of teeth closed by a sliding tab.
usage: The standard British word.
pitfall: Americans say 'zipper' and use 'zip' for a zip code.
examples: The zip on my coat's broken.
Can you do my zip up?

gloss: A small metal fastener of two parts pressed together.
usage: Common British term; 'press stud' is more formal.
examples: The baby's sleepsuit has poppers down the front.
One of the poppers has come off.

gloss: Costumes worn to a party, dressing up as a character or theme.
usage: Standard British term; a 'fancy dress party' is a costume party.
pitfall: 'Fancy dress' does not mean elegant clothing.
examples: It's a fancy dress party — come as a pirate.
He went in fancy dress as a superhero.

gloss: Neat, stylish and well-dressed.
usage: Used for clothing and dress codes: 'smart casual'.
pitfall: In the US 'smart' usually means clever; in Britain it often means well-dressed.
examples: You look very smart today.
The dress code is smart casual.

gloss: Trousers with a bib and shoulder straps.
usage: Standard British term for this garment, worn by children or as fashion.
pitfall: British 'overalls' are a protective work garment.
examples: She looks cute in her little dungarees.
Denim dungarees are back in fashion.

gloss: A loose one-piece garment worn over clothes to protect them while working.
usage: Used for work clothing; 'boiler suit' is also common.
pitfall: In the US 'overalls' are what Britons call dungarees.
examples: The mechanic wore blue overalls.
Put some overalls on before you start painting.

gloss: A sleeveless dress worn over a blouse or jumper.
usage: Common for school uniforms and children's clothes; often 'pinafore dress'.
pitfall: In the US this is a 'jumper', which in Britain is a sweater.
examples: She wore a navy pinafore to school.
A pinafore dress looks lovely over a striped top.

gloss: A soft rounded cap with a short brim at the front.
usage: Strongly associated with northern England and the countryside.
pragmatic_note: Traditionally linked to working-class northern men, now also fashionable.
examples: Grandad never went out without his flat cap.
He wore a tweed flat cap.

gloss: A waterproof jacket made of waxed cotton, often olive green.
usage: Classic countryside wear in Britain.
pragmatic_note: Associated with rural, upper-middle-class style.
examples: He wore his wax jacket to walk the dogs.
A wax jacket and wellies — very country.

gloss: A knitted woolly hat with a pompom on top.
usage: Common British term; 'woolly hat' for one without a bobble.
examples: Wrap up warm and wear your bobble hat.
He looked silly in a bobble hat.

gloss: A close-fitting woollen hood covering the head and neck, leaving the face partly open.
usage: Common word for this winter garment.
examples: Kids used to wear balaclavas to school in winter.
He pulled on his balaclava for the cold.

gloss: Women's plain smart shoes with a moderate heel and no fastening.
usage: Standard British term for office or formal shoes.
pitfall: In Britain 'pumps' are flat canvas or ballet shoes.
examples: She wore navy court shoes to the interview.
I need some comfortable court shoes.

gloss: A shop selling donated second-hand goods to raise money for charity.
usage: A familiar part of every British high street.
pragmatic_note: Charity-shop finds are a point of pride for bargain hunters.
examples: I found this coat in a charity shop.
Take the old clothes to the charity shop.

gloss: A piece of absorbent material worn by a baby to hold urine and faeces.
usage: The only everyday British word; 'diaper' sounds American.
examples: Can you change the baby's nappy?
We go through so many nappies.

gloss: A bag for carrying nappies, wipes and baby essentials.
usage: Standard British term among parents.
examples: The wipes are in the changing bag.
Don't forget the changing bag!

gloss: A rubber or plastic teat given to a baby to suck for comfort.
usage: The everyday British word; 'soother' is also used.
pitfall: In Britain 'dummy' also means a mannequin, or informally a silly person.
examples: He won't sleep without his dummy.
She threw her dummy out of the pram.

gloss: A baby carriage in which a baby lies flat, pushed by hand.
usage: Common British word; often used loosely for any pushchair.
examples: She pushed the pram round the park.
The pram won't fit in the car boot.

gloss: A folding chair on wheels in which a toddler sits.
usage: Standard British term; 'buggy' is the informal equivalent.
examples: Fold up the pushchair before you get on the bus.
He fell asleep in his pushchair.

gloss: A light folding pushchair.
usage: Very common informal British word.
pitfall: In the US a 'buggy' can mean a baby carriage or a horse-drawn cart.
examples: Is there a lift for the buggy?
She's bought a lightweight buggy for holidays.

gloss: A baby's bed with high barred sides.
usage: The standard British word.
pitfall: In the US a 'cot' is a camp bed; Britons call a 'crib' a cot.
examples: The baby's fast asleep in her cot.
We've moved the cot into the nursery.

gloss: A light folding bed, used for guests or camping.
usage: Standard British term.
pitfall: Americans call this a 'cot', which in Britain is a baby's bed.
examples: You can sleep on the camp bed in the lounge.
We put up a camp bed for my cousin.

gloss: A light woven basket with handles, used as a bed for a newborn baby.
usage: Common British term for a newborn's first bed.
examples: She sleeps in a Moses basket next to our bed.
We were given a Moses basket by my sister.

gloss: An all-in-one stretchy garment for a baby, covering body, arms and legs.
usage: Common British term, from an old brand name; 'sleepsuit' is also used.
pitfall: In Britain 'onesie' usually means an adult's all-in-one lounging suit.
examples: Put him in a clean babygrow.
We were given dozens of babygrows.

gloss: A square of thin cotton used to wipe or protect from a baby's sick.
usage: Every British parent has a stack of 'muslins'.
examples: Put a muslin over your shoulder when you wind her.
Pass me a muslin — he's been sick.

gloss: To pat a baby's back to bring up trapped air after feeding.
usage: The British verb is 'wind the baby'; the noun 'wind' means trapped air.
pitfall: Americans 'burp' the baby; pronounced like 'the wind blows'.
examples: Can you wind her after her bottle?
He's crying because he's got wind.

gloss: Mother.
usage: The standard British spelling and pronunciation.
pitfall: 'Mom' is American; Midlands English has 'mom' too, but 'mum' is standard.
examples: I'll ask my mum.
Mum, where are my trainers?

gloss: Child's word for mother.
usage: Used by young children, and by some adults in upper-middle-class families.
pragmatic_note: Adults saying 'Mummy' can sound posh in Britain.
pitfall: Also means an embalmed body, as in Egyptian mummies.
examples: Mummy, can I have a biscuit?
Go and give Mummy a hug.

gloss: Grandmother.
usage: Very common, especially in working-class and southern families; also 'nana'.
pragmatic_note: 'Nan', 'gran', 'granny' and 'grandma' vary by family and region.
examples: We're going to my nan's for Sunday lunch.
My nan's ninety next week.

gloss: Grandmother.
usage: Common, especially in Scotland and the north; 'granny' is affectionate.
examples: My gran taught me to knit.
Gran's coming to stay at Christmas.

gloss: A place where young children are cared for while parents work.
usage: Used for childcare before school; also a baby's bedroom.
pitfall: Not a plant nursery in this context; 'nursery school' is for ages three to four.
examples: She goes to nursery three days a week.
We've decorated the nursery in yellow.

gloss: A place where babies and young children are looked after while parents are busy nearby.
usage: Used for short-term childcare at gyms, shopping centres or workplaces.
pitfall: Pronounced 'kresh'.
examples: The gym has a crèche for members.
Leave the kids in the crèche while we shop.

gloss: A registered person who looks after other people's children in their own home.
usage: Common British childcare option, regulated by Ofsted in England.
pitfall: Different from a 'babysitter', who looks after children in your home for an evening.
examples: Our childminder picks the kids up from school.
We found a lovely childminder down the road.

gloss: A small bowl used as a toilet by young children.
usage: Universal word in British parenting; 'potty training' is the process.
examples: He's just started using the potty.
We're in the middle of potty training.

gloss: A structure of bars for children to climb on.
usage: Found in parks, school playgrounds and gardens.
examples: The kids love the climbing frame at the park.
We've put a climbing frame in the garden.

gloss: A long plank balanced in the middle, on which children sit at each end and rise and fall.
usage: Standard British word in playgrounds.
examples: Let's go on the see-saw.
The see-saw's broken again.

gloss: A shallow pit or box filled with sand for children to play in.
usage: Standard British term in gardens and playgrounds.
pitfall: 'Sandbox' is American and also a tech term.
examples: The kids spent all afternoon in the sandpit.
Cover the sandpit so the cats don't use it.

gloss: A shallow inflatable or plastic pool for young children.
usage: Common on hot days in British gardens; also shallow pools in parks.
pitfall: To 'paddle' in Britain is to walk in shallow water, not to use a paddle.
examples: Let's blow up the paddling pool.
The kids were splashing in the paddling pool.

gloss: A miniature toy house for dolls.
usage: Traditional British form with the apostrophe; 'doll's house' is also used.
examples: She's had the same dolls' house since she was five.
Grandad built a dolls' house for her.

gloss: A game for two players who mark Os and Xs on a grid of nine squares.
usage: The standard British name, played by children everywhere.
examples: We played noughts and crosses on the train.
Fancy a game of noughts and crosses?

gloss: A picture cut into interlocking pieces to be fitted together.
usage: Britons usually say just 'jigsaw'; a family Christmas staple.
examples: We did a thousand-piece jigsaw over Christmas.
There's a piece missing from the jigsaw.

gloss: A book of outline pictures for children to colour in.
usage: Common British term with British spelling.
examples: Bring a colouring book for the long drive.
Adult colouring books were a big trend.

gloss: A small amount of money given regularly to a child by their parents.
usage: The standard British term in families.
examples: She saves her pocket money for sweets.
How much pocket money do you give the kids?

gloss: A mobile phone.
usage: Common British word; most people now just say 'phone'.
pitfall: 'Cell phone' sounds American; 'mobile' is pronounced 'MOH-byle'.
examples: I'll ring you on your mobile.
What's your mobile number?

gloss: A bag carried by women for personal items such as keys and money.
usage: The standard British word.
pitfall: In Britain a 'purse' is a small wallet for coins and cards.
examples: My keys are in my handbag.
She's lost her handbag on the bus.

gloss: A small pouch or wallet, especially a woman's, for money and cards.
usage: Standard British meaning.
pitfall: False friend: in the US a 'purse' is a handbag.
examples: I've left my purse at home.
She took a fiver out of her purse.

gloss: A small pouch on a belt worn around the waist.
usage: Common British term, sometimes used jokingly of tourists.
pitfall: Never use the American term: 'fanny' is a vulgar word in British English.
examples: He wore a bum bag for his passport.
Bum bags are back in fashion.

gloss: A bag carried on the back with shoulder straps.
usage: Common British term, especially for hiking; 'backpack' is also used.
examples: Pack your waterproof in your rucksack.
He set off with a heavy rucksack.

gloss: A large soft bag for carrying clothes when travelling.
usage: Standard British word.
examples: I've packed my gym kit in a holdall.
He threw his holdall in the boot.

gloss: An umbrella.
usage: Common informal British word.
pragmatic_note: Britons carry a brolly 'just in case' almost year-round.
examples: Take a brolly — it's going to rain.
I've left my brolly on the train.

gloss: Glasses for seeing.
usage: Common informal British word.
examples: Have you seen my specs?
I need new specs.

gloss: Glasses for correcting eyesight.
usage: Formal or old-fashioned; used by opticians and in writing.
examples: Spectacles must be worn for driving.
He peered over his spectacles.

gloss: Rings, necklaces and other ornaments worn on the body.
usage: British spelling 'jewellery'; pronounced 'JOO-uhl-ree'.
pitfall: British spelling has a double 'l' and 'ery'.
examples: She keeps her jewellery in a box on the dressing table.
He makes silver jewellery.

gloss: A ring on which keys are kept together.
usage: Standard British word; souvenir keyrings are common gifts.
examples: I've got a little torch on my keyring.
Put the spare key on a separate keyring.

gloss: An insulated container for keeping drinks hot or cold.
usage: Common British word; 'Thermos' also used.
pragmatic_note: A flask of tea is standard kit for British walks and picnics.
pitfall: In the US 'flask' usually means a hip flask for spirits.
examples: We took a flask of tea on the walk.
Fill the flask with hot soup.

gloss: An insulated box for keeping food and drink cold.
usage: Standard British term for picnics and camping.
examples: Pack the sandwiches in the cool box.
The cool box is in the boot.

gloss: An inflatable mattress used for floating on water or as a spare bed.
usage: Common British term, from an old brand name.
examples: The kids floated around the pool on a lilo.
You can sleep on the lilo.
